name: Lucebox Megakernel (single-launch CUDA forward pass for Qwen 3.5-0.8B)
baseline: llama.cpp (BF16, CUDA backend) and PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers (BF16)
workload: Batch-1 prefill of 520 tokens (pp520) and decode of 128 tokens (tg128) for Qwen 3.5-0.8B in BF16 on an RTX 3090, with all 24 layers fused into one persistent CUDA kernel launch.
claimed_speedup: RTX 3090 RESULTS.md: prefill pp520 21,347 tok/s vs llama.cpp BF16 11,247 (README states 1.9x) and PyTorch HF 7,578; decode tg128 413 tok/s vs llama.cpp 267 (1.55x) and PyTorch HF 108 (3.8x). Also 1.87 tok/J at a 220 W power limit.
compiler_and_flags: setup.py: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_<auto-detected, sm_86 for RTX 3090> --use_fast_math -std=c++17 plus NUM_BLOCKS/BLOCK_SIZE defines; host -O3; CUDA toolkit version for the RTX 3090 run not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 24GB (also RTX 2080 Ti, DGX Spark GB10 and Apple M5 Max 36GB for the efficiency comparison); host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Hard-wired to one small hybrid DeltaNet/attention model (Qwen 3.5-0.8B); batch size 1 only (README says to use vLLM or SGLang for batched throughput); BF16 on Ampere (FP16 path for Turing, NVFP4 path for Blackwell); built as a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension, so it is not a general kernel library.
caveats: First-party benchmark. llama.cpp baseline is 'latest release at time of testing, default settings' with no version or commit, and no host CPU is stated. The model is only 0.8B parameters, where per-token kernel-launch overhead dominates and llama.cpp has no fused DeltaNet path, so the result may not transfer to larger models. The 413 tok/s decode figure is quoted at a 220 W power limit while llama.cpp is quoted at 350 W, which if anything understates the gap. A search summary of the HN thread quoted 37,800 tok/s prefill, which differs from the 21,347 on RESULTS.md; only RESULTS.md numbers are used here. HN thread itself not opened (egress blocked); the repo was renamed from luce-megakernel to lucebox and now also hosts speculative-decoding projects (DFlash, PFlash) not assessed here.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN megakernel fused CUDA LLM inference faster than llama.cpp vLLM PyTorch open source kernels' surfaced item 47691182 'Show HN: OS Megakernel that match M5 Max Tok/w at 2x the Throughput on RTX 3090'; project opened on github.com.

name: sgemm.cu (hand-tuned FP32 GEMM for NVIDIA GA102/Ampere GPUs)
workload: FP32 SGEMM, NN layout, square m=n=k from 1024 to about 12800 in steps of 128, RTX 3090, with clocks unlocked and with clocks locked at 1395 MHz, both at 350 W.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no text numbers, only two plots (assets/perf.png, perf_locked.png). Reading them by eye at m=n=k near 12800: about 25,300-25,500 GFLOP/s vs cuBLAS about 24,300 with unlocked clocks (about 4-5% faster), and about 23,000-23,500 vs about 21,800 with locked 1395 MHz clocks (about 6-7% faster); approximate, derived from page data. The HN title claims 'up to 24% faster than cuBLAS on a 4090' (snippet only, not on the repo page).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc V12.6.85 (CUDA 12.6), g++ 13.3, CMake 3.28.3; CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86 with separable compilation; no explicit -O flags in CMakeLists.txt (the -O3 lines are commented out).
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (driver 550.120), Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS; host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: FP32 SGEMM only, and the README documents only the NN case; tuned and tested for RTX 3090 (GA102), expected to be fast on Ada/Ampere/Volta/Turing; it is a benchmark and test harness rather than a packaged library.
caveats: Benchmark code is public (benchmark.sh, CMake) and cuBLAS is run in the same harness, so this would be tier A except that the host CPU model and nvcc optimisation flags are not stated and the numbers exist only as images. Margins in the plots are small (single-digit percent) at large sizes and sgemm.cu is slower than cuBLAS at small sizes (for example near m=n=k=1280 about 17,000 vs about 19,300 GFLOP/s unlocked). The 24% on an RTX 4090 claim from the HN title is not reproduced on the repo page, which shows RTX 3090 only. Repo identity was inferred from the HN title and README content (HN thread not opened); the same plots also show a Simon Boehm / tinyBLAS kernel at about 16,500 GFLOP/s, which is slower than cuBLAS.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN CUDA kernel faster than cuDNN cuBLAS attention softmax from scratch' surfaced item 41122018 'Show HN: FP32 matmul of large matrices up to 24% faster than cuBLAS on a 4090'; repo located by title and verified on github.com.

name: Effort (bucketMul approximate matrix multiplication for LLM inference on Apple Silicon)
baseline: Apple MPS default matrix multiplication (benchmark.swift labels it 'comparable to llama.cpp')
workload: Weight-matrix multiplication during LLM inference on Apple Silicon, timed by benchmarks/benchmark.swift at several 'effort' levels against the default MPS matmul.
claimed_speedup: README: 'At 50% effort, it performs as fast as regular matrix multiplications on Apple Silicon chips; at 25% effort, it is twice as fast while still retaining most of the quality.'
hardware: 'Apple Silicon chips'; the specific chip is not stated in the README or benchmark.swift.
tradeoffs: Approximate computation: it skips the least important weights, so quality drops as effort falls; needs converted weights; written in Swift and Metal for macOS only, with no C++ API; the author describes it as a demo with 'ton of things to fix'.
caveats: First-party claim with no hardware, model size or raw timings in the repo; the benchmark script prints timings only when run. At 50% effort the claim is only parity with regular matmul. The author notes real generation speed is slower than the matmul benchmark because of implementation overhead. The quality claim ('most of the quality') was not checked, and the project page and blog (kolinko.github.io) are egress-blocked. Last commit is 2024-07-01. Repo identity inferred from the HN title and README (HN thread not opened).

name: flash-attention-minimal (forward-only FlashAttention in about 100 lines of CUDA)
baseline: naive PyTorch attention (eager matmul + softmax + matmul)
workload: One profiled forward call of attention with batch 16, 12 heads, sequence length 64, head dimension 64, FP32, on a T4 (bench.py).
claimed_speedup: README sample output on a T4: manual attention Self CUDA time total 52.545 ms vs minimal flash attention 3.908 ms (about 13x, derived from page data); Self CPU time total 52.389 ms vs 11.452 ms; the README says 'Speed-up achieved!'.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O2 (extra_cuda_cflags=['-O2'] in bench.py via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load); CUDA, PyTorch and compiler versions not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA T4 (AWS g4 instance); host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Educational forward pass only (no backward); FP32 rather than FP16; block size fixed at 32 at compile time; one thread per output row, which makes the matmuls slow.
caveats: Weak evidence. The win is only over a naive eager PyTorch attention at deliberately tiny sizes: a comment in bench.py says 'Use small model params, otherwise slower than manual attention', and the README admits it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes. Each variant is timed with a single profiled call and no warm-up is visible in bench.py, so one-time CUDA/cuBLAS initialisation may inflate the manual attention figure. No comparison with cuDNN, the official flash-attention or PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention. A 'tensorcore' branch exists but was not assessed. Repo identity inferred from the HN title (HN thread not opened).
